title: Asha and the Playground Planets
markdown:
The museum room was hushed, twilight filtering through tall windows. Long gentle shadows stretched across polished wood. Asha sat with her two dearest friends: Tumble the goat, wool as soft as a newly fallen cloud, and Professor Imani, whose voice was a slow warm river, eyes crinkling like dry leaves.

They gathered around a delicate model of the solar system, tiny spheres on almost invisible wires, dancing so neatly tucked.

“It looks so close together,” Tumble murmured. “They’re all just… here.”

Imani smiled. “Our eyes can play tricks. The real sky holds so much more space than a little model can show.”

Asha nodded. “I wish we could show how far apart everything really is, and how small the planets are compared with all that empty in-between. I tried to draw it. Scattered dots on a very big plain page. It didn’t feel vast enough.”

Tumble nudged a tiny reddish bead, then a larger lumpy one. “This is Jupiter. Biggest. And this tiny one is Earth. On the table they look almost the same size.”

Asha held the Earth bead between thumb and finger. Light. Small. She looked at the high ceilings, the long shadows. A shy seed of a thought.

“What if we used something much bigger than this table? The playground. We don’t need to measure perfectly. We just need to feel how far apart they are.”

Imani leaned forward. “A grand idea. The meadows can be our canvas.”

They carried a bag of beads into the cooling evening. Asha set a bright yellow marble for the Sun at the near edge of the playground, where the grass still held the day’s warmth. “Sun first. Then we walk outward.”

Mercury: a grey speck, only a few steps away. Venus a little further. Earth — their home bead — still close enough that Tumble could bleat at both sun and earth without raising his voice. Mars, ruddy, a bit more of a stroll. The gaps grew like ripples on a still pond, but they were still a family of inner worlds.

Then Jupiter. Asha held up a swirling brown-and-orange marble that seemed to hold storms in its tiny form. “Much, much further. The inner worlds were a neighbourhood. This is a journey.”

They walked. And walked. The playground, which had always been a place for chasing and falling over, stretched into something quieter. Swing-chains ticked behind them and then were too far to hear. Tumble paused to nibble a particularly sweet blade of grass, then trotted to where Asha pointed, his hooves making small honest sounds in the cooling earth. Professor Imani’s walking stick was a slow steady guide, tapping once when the next bead should sit. Saturn came after a long breath, rings like a delicate halo of thread, a truly beautiful smallness. Then Uranus, a soft pale blue that looked colder than the evening. Finally Neptune, deep and tranquil, at the very edge of the open field, like a guardian of the farthest reaches.

Asha stood at the end with Neptune in her palm and did not speak. The evening breeze moved the leaves. Crickets tried a first shy note, then another. She looked back across the vast green toward the yellow sun-marble. It was only a thought of yellow now. Mercury was lost. Earth was a maybe, a guess she could not prove without walking all the way home. The space between her shoes and that first sun felt like a kind of kindness — room enough for everyone, and no one crowded. The vastness settled around them like a blanket woven from starlight and silence. Tumble leaned on her knee and watched a single moth, which was, for a moth, exactly the right size.

“Even though the beads are so small,” she said at last, “look at the space between. The playground feels huge when we run. Out here it is showing us how much quiet room there is. Tiny marbles on a giant silent field. Farther than our eyes usually bother to imagine.”

Imani’s gaze swept the grass. “Not close neighbours in a crowd. Distant friends, each on its own path. This field helps the mind wander into the true scale.”

Tumble nudged Asha’s hand, his simple way of saying he understood, and did not try to make Jupiter look bigger than it was — only farther, which was wonder enough.

The moon rose, a silver sliver in deep velvet, and even that sliver seemed to understand about distances. They gathered the beads slowly, leaving the gaps behind them in the dark, each planet returning to a pocket that was far too small for the walk it had just taken. Homeward, the museum windows held a last of the rose-gold. Beds would feel, tonight, like a very small inner planet, snug beside a sun that had already gone in. Asha wondered what else might be hiding in ordinary size — a pebble, a hill, a sky — if you gave it enough grass to tell the truth. Tumble bleated once, softly, as if filing the field under Vast, and Imani’s stick tapped the path in time with their tired, contented feet.
characters: Asha (a museum helper), Tumble (a goat), Imani (a professor)
